name: Metallic Green
lede: Metallic Green is a dark olive from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; despite the name, the swatch is closer to olive brown than to green, and the copper greens that painters called metallic are a different thing.

sections.title: A dictionary name
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* (1930) lists Metallic Green at plate 15, position L 6, with 1928 as its earliest use, and the NBS Circular 553 of 1955 cites it [1]. The nearest ISCC-NBS category is moderate olive, only 1.6 units away [1]. Its neighbors are [[antique-bronze]], [[olive]] and [[oil-green]] [2].

Painters used the same words for something else. Pastoureau notes that Poussin made artificial metallic greens by treating strips of copper with acid, lime or vinegar; the pigment was splendid but unstable, corrosive and toxic [3]. Vermeer avoided it [3]. Nothing links that pigment to this swatch, whose name is simply the dictionary's [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Metallic Green appears in 483 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 2.0%, as photographed [5]. It peaks in paintings of the 1800s, in 131 of 8,345 (1.6%), 1.4 times the rate expected from the same museums [5]. The painter most devoted to it is Karl Isakson, in 6 of 21 works here [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [5].
